activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Feeling homesick while away from home is very common; nearly everyone misses something about home when they are away.
story:
Riley had never slept at anyone's house before, so he packed like he might be gone a month: two flashlights, a water bottle, three granola bars, and the small plastic dinosaur he had kept on his nightstand since he was six, buried at the bottom of the bag where nobody would see it. Harper met him at the door already holding a controller, and the evening went by fast, pizza and a racing game and Harper's dog stealing a sock. It was only after the lights went out, in the green glow of Harper's star projector, that Riley noticed the strange tight feeling in his chest.

It was an anomaly, that was the problem. Everything here was good, and he still felt like something was wrong, like he'd left a light on at home and couldn't go back to switch it off. He stared at the ceiling stars and tested an idea in his head, the way he tested ideas in science class. Maybe the feeling needed a reason, and if he found the reason, it would stop. He reviewed the evening piece by piece. The pizza had been fine. The racing game had been fine. He'd won twice, even.

Beside him, Harper turned over with a sigh.

"Can't sleep either?" Riley whispered.

"No." Harper's voice was small in the dark. "I always get like this at sleepovers. I got it really bad at camp last summer. I wrote my mom a letter the first night and everything." Harper paused. "It's called being homesick. Basically everybody misses something about home when they're away somewhere. The camp counselor said even she gets it."

Riley sat up a little. "Everybody?"

"Pretty much, yeah." Harper pulled a folded paper out from under the pillow and held it near the glow. It was a photograph of a fat orange cat. "I bring this. Meet Biscuit. It helps a little."

Riley considered the photograph, then reached into his bag, past the flashlights, and set the plastic dinosaur on the blanket between them. "His name is Fang. He sits on my nightstand."

"Fang is awesome," said Harper, with complete sincerity.

They arranged the two animals side by side, facing the door like guards, and Harper's breathing slowed within minutes, but Riley stayed awake a while longer doing the math. If nearly everyone missed home when they were away, then the tight feeling in his chest wasn't an anomaly at all. It was just what happened, like getting cold without a jacket. He could stop hunting for a broken reason. That thought arrived quietly and settled him more than the dinosaur did.

In the morning, Harper's mom made chocolate-chip pancakes, and Harper asked, in an abrupt rush before Riley could take the first bite, "Same time next month? You could bring a different dinosaur. Fang could have a friend."

Riley bit into the pancake. "Two dinosaurs," he said. "Fang doesn't travel alone."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The sports bar was so loud that Noemie had to lean across the nachos to hear her uncle. On the giant screen, luminous under the dim lights, a quarterback's name glowed beside the number 158.3. Her uncle groaned. "Perfect game," he said, "and they give him one hundred fifty-eight point three. Why not a hundred? Who invents a number like that?" The clock on the broadcast showed two minutes left in the half, and Noemie's father had promised they would leave at halftime to get her to Anas's birthday party on time. Two minutes, she thought, was actually a lot of minutes.

She remembered Ms. Jean-Louis's class in September, when the whole week's news had been squeezed into one chart on the board. Ms. Jean-Louis had said numbers like that were built, not found, and Noemie had written in her notebook: one number can carry many events. Maybe that was what this strange number was doing. She pulled out her phone and texted Anas, whose father watched every game: "why is a perfect passer rating 158.3 and not 100?"

Anas answered before the two-minute warning. "It's called passer rating. It combines several passing statistics into one number." Then a second message: "Scale is 0 at the bottom. Max is 158.3. That's just where the top is." Noemie read it twice. So the number wasn't a score out of a hundred, like a test. It was a ranking generated from a whole pile of separate plays, all the completions and yards and everything else, pressed together into a single figure so people at a bar could compare quarterbacks in five seconds.

"Uncle Dev," she said, "it's not out of a hundred. It's its own scale, zero to one hundred fifty-eight point three." Her uncle squinted at the screen, then at her. "Huh," he said. "So a hundred wouldn't mean perfect." He had been complaining about the number for a quarter of play, and now he shrugged and reached for a chip. At halftime her father signaled toward the door, and Noemie slid the last nacho onto her plate. On her way out she glanced back at the screen, where the number 158.3 still hung beside the quarterback's name, alone, as if it had always made sense.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: According to the American Academy of Dermatology, about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne.
story:
Nora sat in the waiting room with her mother, pretending to read a poster about sun safety while really she was thinking about Charlotte. Yesterday Charlotte had scooted her desk away and said, not quietly enough, that somebody smelled like a locker room. Nora had wanted to sink through the floor. Now she was here for her ten-year checkup, and she had a plan: she would ask the doctor her real question without her mother hearing, which meant she had to negotiate a moment alone.

When the nurse called her back, Nora was agile about it. "Mom, can I go in by myself? I'm ten now." Her mother shrugged and stayed with the magazines.

The doctor turned out to be a woman named Ms. Bouchard, who listened to Nora's heart, then asked if she had any questions. Nora took a breath. "My armpits smell, and I got my first pimple, and my friend was grossed out. Is something wrong with me?"

Ms. Bouchard shook her head. "Your body is starting puberty. Sweat glands get busier, oil glands too. Daily shower, deodorant every morning, and wash your face." She tapped the chart in her hand. "And about pimples. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne."

Nora stared at her. Eighty-five percent. She did the math in her head: that was almost everybody, not just kids with greasy hair or bad luck. Even kids like Tate, who seemed to have perfect skin, would probably count eventually. Charlotte would count too. Maybe Charlotte already did, under the concealer Nora had noticed last week.

"Almost everyone?" Nora asked.

"Minor or more," said Ms. Bouchard. "It's practically a rule of growing up."

In the car, Nora asked her mother to stop at the drugstore. She picked out a deodorant that smelled like cucumber and set it on the counter, money from her allowance ready in her fist.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
story:
Nolan lined up at the baseline of the outdoor court behind the gym, ball tucked under one arm, and counted the players ahead of him. Fourteen kids, twelve spots. The October wind had stripped the trees along the fence, leaving the branches bare and the court's edges littered with dry leaves that skittered like small animals whenever a gust came through.

The tryout drills started fast. Suicides first, then layup lines, then a three-on-three game that the coach said would run for twenty minutes without stopping. Nolan had planned for this. He'd read an article in his uncle's sports magazine last summer about a swimmer who forgot her water bottle and faded badly in the last heat of her tryouts. The article said that losing about 2 percent of your body weight in sweat, without drinking enough to replace it, can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events. He hadn't fully believed it then. He'd been sitting on a porch with a lemonade in his hand, and it had seemed like something that happened to other people.

Now he kept his blue bottle at the sideline and drank at every break, even short ones. His friend Tyrell laughed at him between sprints. "You drink more than my goldfish," Tyrell said, gasping through a grin.

"Watch Lilith," Nolan said quietly, nodding toward the far basket. Lilith had come to tryouts straight from helping her mother unload a van, and Nolan had noticed she hadn't brought any water. In the first drill she'd been the fastest kid on the court. By the third sprint she was still quick but her layups had gone flat, bouncing hard off the back rim. In the three-on-three game, she stopped calling for the ball.

Nolan kept tracking her while he guarded his own man. There was a pattern, and it wasn't her skill disappearing all at once. It drained away in stages, like water through a crack. He remembered the swimmer in the article, how she had led her heat until the final laps and then simply slowed, and how the writer had laid out the numbers as if they were a law of physics. Sweat out too much, drink too little, and the body pays for it exactly when the event runs long. This game was long. The coach kept the clock running through fouls and out-of-bounds, and the sun, though mild, sat right on the blacktop.

At the next whistle, Nolan jogged to the sideline, filled his bottle at the fountain, and carried it over during the water break. "Drink," he said, holding it out. "You were beating everybody twenty minutes ago."

Lilith looked at the bottle, then at him, and drank half of it in one long pull. In the last five minutes of the game she cut to the basket twice, caught a pass she would have missed earlier, and laid the ball in soft off the glass. The coach wrote something on his clipboard.

When the whistle finally sounded, Tyrell collapsed dramatically on the barren patch of dirt beyond the sideline, and Lilith sat down beside him, still holding Nolan's bottle. The coach began reading names. He read slowly, as if he wanted to sustain the suspense on purpose, and Nolan felt his own heart working hard against his ribs.

"Nolan," the coach said, and then, a few names later, "Lilith."

Lilith stood up and handed the bottle back, and the wind pushed a leaf across the line at her feet.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Japanese uses different family words for your own family and someone else's: you call your own mother "haha" when talking to others, but a friend's mother is "okaasan."
story:
Jonathan had a plan: by the end of Japanese class, he would describe his entire family, plus the goldfish, in full sentences, and Mr. McKenzie would be so impressed he would forget about the homework Jonathan forgot. He practiced under his breath all through lunch. "Watashi no haha wa sushi ga suki desu. My mother likes sushi." Filip, sitting one row over, kept trying to distract him by making laser noises with his pencil, which he claimed was a "radical space pen."

The trouble started when Filip went first. "Watashi no okaasan wa pizza ga suki desu," Filip said proudly. My pizza-loving mother, in perfect sentence form. Jonathan filed that away. Okaasan. That must be the word for mother. His own sentence used haha because that was what the worksheet example happened to say, but okaasan sounded far more impressive, like a word with a good haircut.

When his turn came, Jonathan cleared his throat. "Watashi no okaasan wa karaoke ga suki desu," he announced, meaning his own mother loved karaoke, which was terrifyingly true.

Amine put her hand over her mouth. She was laughing so hard her chair squeaked. "You just called your own mom okaasan," she said. "Okaasan is for other people's moms. You say haha when you talk about your own mother to someone else."

Jonathan stared at the worksheet. So that was why the example said haha. Filip hadn't been wrong at all, because Filip had been describing his own mother with haha only after Mr. McKenzie's careful correction, which Jonathan had been too busy with his space-pen rivalry to hear. Like a tiny detective, he extracted the rule from the wreckage: haha for mine, okaasan for yours. He tried again, slower this time. "Watashi no haha wa karaoke ga suki desu. Watashi no haha wa totemo genki desu."

"Better," said Amine. "Now the goldfish."

"Watashi no sakana wa... " Jonathan paused. The goldfish, a radical orange creature named Steve, was technically his sister's. He raised his hand. "Mr. McKenzie, whose fish counts as whose family?"

"Try both," Mr. McKenzie said, fighting a smile.

Filip leaned over and whispered, "Steve no haha wa dare desu ka."

activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: In an atom, protons and neutrons are packed together in a tiny central nucleus, and electrons move in the space around the nucleus.
story:
Charlie had planned to finish her atom model on Thursday, but the science fair was moved up to Wednesday, so she stayed after school with her box of supplies spread across the lab table.

Ryder sat down across from her, spinning a pencil like a tiny propeller. "You're doing oxygen, right? That's eight protons?"

"Eight protons, eight neutrons, eight electrons," Charlie said, and she flourished her paintbrush over the styrofoam balls like a magician. The protons were red, the neutrons blue, and the electrons were small yellow beads on wire. She had already glued the red and blue ones into a tight cluster, and now she was pressing the yellow beads into the same cluster, one by one.

Alena leaned over from the next table, where she was lettering her poster. She frowned at Charlie's model. "Wait. Why are the yellow ones in the middle?"

"Because that's where everything goes," Charlie said. "I glued the protons and neutrons together, so I just kept going."

Alena set down her marker. "Ryder, didn't the diagram in the book have the electrons out on those ring things?"

Ryder stopped spinning his pencil. He flipped through his notebook until he found a page he'd copied from the textbook. "Yeah. Look." He turned it toward Charlie. The picture showed the protons and neutrons packed into a small ball in the center, with electrons orbiting way out in the space around it, like planets circling a sun.

Charlie stared at the drawing, then at her model. All her yellow beads were buried in the middle. She tried to remember what Ms. Nielsen had said on Monday, but she'd been half-listening while sharpening pencils. "So the protons and neutrons are in the middle," she said slowly, "and the electrons are around the outside?"

"That's what the diagram shows," Alena said.

Charlie tested the idea against the picture. If the red and blue balls belonged in a tight center, then her yellow beads needed wire loops, like the rings in the drawing. The middle was only for protons and neutrons. She plucked the beads back out, one at a time, wincing when two left glue dents in the foam.

Ryder pulled a coil of craft wire from his own supply box without being asked. "You can have this. I have extra." He bent the first loop into a circle while Alena trimmed the wire ends so they wouldn't poke anyone's fingers.

Charlie threaded the electrons onto the rings and wired the rings to a stick so they circled the nucleus. When she spun the top ring gently, the little yellow beads slid around like they were flying.

Ms. Nielsen walked past on her way out and paused at the table. "Nucleus," Charlie said, pointing to the red and blue cluster. "And the electrons go around it."

Ms. Nielsen smiled and gave her a thumbs-up on her way to the door.

Charlie turned the model slowly in her hands, watching the electrons circle the center. "It actually looks like something sophisticated now," she said, and set it in the middle of the table where the judges would see it first.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.
story:
Matthew carried the cardboard box across the backyard carefully, the way you carry a full glass of water. Inside, Rusty, his brand-new guinea pig, sniffed at the air holes. The hutch stood under the maple tree, and the grass around it was still lush from all the rain that week, though the patch under the hutch had begun to deteriorate, going thin and brown where the shadow sat all day. Matthew set the box down, opened the flap, and waited. Rusty stepped out, whiskered the new world, and settled in.

That first night, Matthew heard it from his bedroom window: a steady, metallic scraping. Ting, ting, ting. In the morning he checked the hutch. The bars on one corner were shiny where something had been chewing them, and Rusty sat right there, working at the wire with quick little bites. Matthew frowned. There was food in the bowl, fresh water in the bottle, and a handful of clover he had picked himself. So why chew the cage?

He called Margaret, who had kept guinea pigs since second grade. "Is he trying to escape?" Matthew asked. "Mine did that too," Margaret said. "Their front teeth never stop growing, so they have to chew on things to wear them down." Matthew looked at Rusty's mouth. The teeth were small and orange and definitely there, but he could not watch them grow. Still, if they never stopped, that explained the pattern: the cage bars were the only hard thing in the hutch. That had to be it. He remembered the woodshop on Mill Street, which sold scrap boards cheap since the recession had slowed business, and he rode his bike there and came back with two untreated pine blocks.

He wedged the blocks into the corner where the bars were shiny. Then he sat on the grass and watched. Rusty investigated one block, nose twitching, and took an experimental bite. Crunch. He gnawed steadily, wood dust drifting onto the hutch floor, and the metallic tinging stopped. Matthew picked a blade of clover and pushed it through the bars. "Better?" he asked. Rusty's teeth went right on working.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
Mr. Castillo raised his hand for quiet and said the new unit was called "Where We Come From," and today everyone would share one thing about their roots. Everly sank a little in her seat, because her own answer felt boring: born here, grandparents from here, one cousin in Ohio. But when the turn passed to the boy by the window, Niko, the problem got more interesting.

"Where are you from?" Leane asked him, when he hesitated.

"Okay, so," Niko said. "I was born in Egypt. Then Singapore. Then Chile, then the Netherlands. My dad works for a company that moves him." He rubbed the back of his neck. "So, nowhere? I don't know how to answer that."

"That's such an exceptional answer," Leane said. "Four countries!"

"It's not an answer, though," Niko said. "It's a shrug with extra steps."

Mr. Castillo started to speak, but Everly waved her hand so fast her chair squeaked. "Wait. I want to figure this out. Can I ask him stuff instead of telling about my cousin?"

Mr. Castillo nodded, half smiling, and Everly turned around in her seat. She had a theory. If Niko didn't come from any one country, maybe he came from the space between them, like a pattern you couldn't see on a map, only in the person. "Which foods do you miss?" she asked.

He counted on his fingers. "Koshari, chili relleno, this Dutch cookie my neighbor made. And a Singapore chicken rice that I would invest my whole allowance in, if anyone here sold it."

"What do people say you sound like?"

"A bit of everything. Kids used to guess. They were always wrong."

"Then you're not from nowhere," Everly said. "You're from all of it at once." She pulled the class dictionary off the shelf and flipped through it, chewing her pencil, until Leane leaned over and said she'd heard a phrase for this somewhere, in her sister's sociology book. "Third culture kid," Leane read slowly. "It says an American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, coined that term in the 1950s. It's for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Niko said the words to himself, twice, like tasting something. "Third culture kid. So there's a name for it. There's a whole label, and I just never got mine."

"That's your answer for your chart," Everly said, sliding the dictionary across. "I'll write 'Ohio' next to mine. Fair trade."

He grinned and copied the words onto his paper.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, which is why many museums keep delicate items in dim rooms.
story:
The museum's textile gallery was so dim that Leah almost walked past the old quilt hanging in the corner. "How is anybody supposed to see this?" Whitney whispered beside her, squinting at the faded blue stars stitched into its pattern. "It's like the museum wants us to guess."

Leah leaned closer to the case. The quilt's colours were soft and washed out, except in one corner where a deep, unbleached red glowed as if it had been hidden for a century. She glanced up at the ceiling. Every other gallery they had walked through that morning had been bright, with track lights blazing onto the paintings. Here, the only light came from small bulbs set far back in the walls, and heavy curtains sealed the doorway behind them.

"That's weird," she said slowly. "Remember the room with the paper documents? Noel said it felt like a cave in there." She turned in a circle, counting the dim rooms they had passed: the letters, the watercolour sketches, this quilt. Fabric, paper, paintings on delicate surfaces. Then she thought about the stone sculptures and the metal armour in the bright rooms, colours that had not faded at all. A pattern was forming in her head, and she wanted to test it.

She found Mr. Becker near the entrance, guarding the clipboard with the class list. "Mr. Becker, could we ask the guide one thing?" A few minutes later, a woman in a museum badge joined them by the quilt. "We noticed the delicate stuff is all in the dark," Leah said, "and the armour is in the bright rooms. Is the light the reason?"

The guide smiled and nodded. "Light slowly fades the dyes and pigments in textiles, paper and some paintings, so we keep those pieces in dim rooms." Whitney exhaled, relieved that she was not just failing a vision test. The guide led them to a low bench with a lamp and a mirror beside it, letting them angle the reflection toward the quilt's hidden corner.

"Look at that symmetry," Leah whispered. Under the borrowed light, the stars matched perfectly, point for point, and the deep red corner turned out to have a twin on the other side, protected behind a fold of fabric all these years. Whitney copied the design into her notebook for their history project, sketching fast before the lamp clicked off on its timer.

Back in the bright hallway, Noel complained that the whole gallery had an ominous feel, like a haunted house. "It's not creepy," Leah said, pulling out her own notebook. "It's the opposite. Somebody cared enough to keep those colours alive." She underlined her sketch of the twin stars and added one line beneath it: still there.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
Kaitlyn had been at Camp Windigo for exactly six hours, and she already missed her own pillow, her dog, and doors that locked. Her mom had promised the homesick feeling was temporary, but temporary felt like a very long word when you were sleeping in a canvas tent with eleven strangers. At the campfire that night, Mr. Guo announced a challenge before marshmallows: no phones allowed at all this week, which meant the campers lying on the dock afterward had no map, no compass, and no idea which way was north.

"I know a trick with moss," said Yassin, chewing his last marshmallow. "Moss grows on the north side of trees."

"Every tree on this island has moss on all four sides," said Maelly. "It's basically a moss island."

Kaitlyn tilted her head back. The sky above the lake was darker than any sky at home, thick with stars, and the water underneath the dock doubled every one of them. She found the Big Dipper first, because her grandfather had taught her that shape when she was seven. It hung low over the pines, its bowl catching starlight like an actual dipper someone had set down and forgotten. Then she remembered the last thing he had told her, the part she'd half ignored while eating birthday cake.

"The two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl," she said slowly, sitting up, "are called the pointer stars."

"Pointer to what?" Yassin asked.

She lined up her arm with the two stars and stretched it out, up and away from the bowl, five times the distance between them, like her grandfather had shown her with his thumb. Her finger landed on a lone, medium-bright star with nothing crowded around it. "That one. The North Star. So that's north." The dock faced it, which meant the cabins were east, and the dining hall with the good smell of pancakes and the terrible smell of the vaccine clinic forms on the wall was west.

"Prove it," Maelly said.

"Okay. If that's north, and we walk that way along the shore, we should hit the big rock Mr. Guo pointed out on the tour. He said the rock is on the north point." The three of them tiptoed past the tents, flashlight off, and followed the water. Ten minutes of squelching boots later, the rock rose up in front of them, pale against the dark lake, exactly where north should be.

Kaitlyn put her hand on the cold granite to verify it, then looked back up. The Dipper had shifted a little, but her finger still found the same star. "Tomorrow we won't get lost on the canoe trip," she said.

"You realize," said Maelly, "you're the reason we're not homesick anymore."

"Speak for yourself," said Yassin. "I still want my dog. But now I can find my tent from anywhere on Earth, so that's something."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so real feeding relationships form a food web of many linked chains rather than one single chain.
story:
Levi crouched on the nature trail with his notebook balanced on one knee, glaring at a drawing that was supposed to be a food chain. Mr. Charles had assigned it that morning: start with the sun, end with a top predator, and be ready to explain what happens if one link disappears. Levi had drawn the sun, then grass, then a rabbit, then a hawk, with arrows marching in a tidy line. It looked perfect. It also felt wrong, though he couldn't say why, and that itchy feeling had drained his stamina for drawing faster than the uphill walk had.

That's when he spotted Amara by the creek, holding her own notebook at arm's length like it had insulted her. A duck was paddling past her boots, quacking with what Levi considered unreasonable confidence.

"My chain is broken," Amara said. "Sun, pond weed, snail, duck. But I just watched this duck eat the weed too. It ate the plant and the snail. Right there." She pointed at the water, where a bit of pond weed was still drifting, though the snail had, regrettably for the snail, evaporated into the duck.

"So your duck is on two chains," Levi said slowly.

"It can't be. A chain is one line. That's the whole point of a chain." Amara frowned. "Maybe I fail."

Levi picked up a pebble and set it on the path. "Okay, pretend this is the sun." He lined up a stick, a bottle cap, and a pinecone. "Sun, grass, rabbit, hawk. Now your stuff." He added a leaf and a snail shell. "Sun, pond weed, snail, duck. But the duck also eats the weed." He nudged the pinecone and the leaf until they touched. "So they connect."

Amara crouched beside him. "Then nothing is one chain. Everything eats more than one thing. My frog back home eats bugs AND it got eaten by a heron once, I saw it, it was horrifying and also awesome."

"So if the hawks vanish," Levi said, tapping his line, "the rabbits go nuts, but the foxes still eat rabbits too, so it's not a total disaster. Everything has backup snacks." He grinned. "Backup snacks. That's the scientific term."

"It is not," said Quinten, arriving downhill at a jog, out of breath. "What are you doing, playing rocks?"

"Building an argument." Amara stood and brushed off her knees. "We show Mr. Charles that the chains link up. He said a chain, but the duck ate my snail AND my weed, so the truth is bigger than the assignment."

They found Mr. Charles near the trailhead, and Amara held out her notebook with its crossed arrows and added lines. "It's not a chain," she said. "It's a food web."

Mr. Charles raised his eyebrows. "That's exactly the word I was hoping somebody would find."

Quinten leaned over Levi's pebble diagram, tapping the duck. "So if the snails disappear, what happens?"

Levi considered the duck, the weed, the heron that had once been terrifying and great. "The duck survives. She's got options."

Amara wrote one word in the margin, huge, and underlined it three times: web.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
story:
The mosque parking lot was already full when Violet climbed out of the car behind Pablo and his little brother. Streamers hung from the doorway, kids were running with sparkly gift bags, and the whole courtyard smelled like cardamom and syrup. Pablo had invited her that morning with a negotiation: she could come along if she promised not to mention the chocolate cake her mom was baking that afternoon. "Deal," Violet had said, mostly because she wanted to see what a whole month of mysterious lunches had been building up to.

For weeks at school, Pablo had slid his lunch tray away untouched. Violet had guessed he was saving money, then that he hated the cafeteria's pizza, then that he was on some secret soccer diet. None of the guesses fit. Today she watched him eat three pieces of sheer khurma before anyone finished their first, and she felt the pieces click together like a puzzle snapping shut. He hadn't been able to eat all month, and now he could. That was why this morning felt like a holiday and a birthday mashed into one.

"So the fasting is over?" she asked, watching Pablo's grandmother pile a fourth piece onto his plate, and Pablo's brother immediately negotiate for a matching piece of his own.

"Today is Eid al-Fitr," Pablo said through a mouthful. "That means it's the celebration at the end of Ramadan, the month when we fast from dawn until sunset." His little brother nodded solemnly, cheeks packed like a squirrel's.

"Wait," Violet said. "Dawn until sunset? So you couldn't even have a snack at recess?" Pablo shook his head and grinned. Violet tried imagining being hungry while the cafeteria smelled like tacos, and failed. The fasting must have been the nocturnal opposite of everything she'd assumed: not avoiding food, but saving it all up, like the whole month was one long drumroll. When the imam called everyone inside for the prayer, Pablo's grandmother patted the bench beside her, and Violet complied without being asked twice. Pablo leaned over and whispered, "After this, there's a second cake in the car."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
The gym was closed for floor repairs, so the team practiced outside on the cracked court behind the school. It was the stickiest day of the summer, and by the third drill Jade's shirt clung to her back like a wet towel. Gillian, who had made the travel team two years running, kept sprinting as if the air were normal, but even she stood bent over with her hands on her knees halfway through scrimmage.

Jade noticed something odd. Last week they had played in hotter weather, a dry, burning day, and everyone had finished tired but fine. Today was cooler, and yet her legs felt like sandbags and Philemon, who usually ran circles around everybody, kept asking for substitutions. She spun the ball on her finger while she thought, then bounced it hard and caught it.

"Sweat," she said to Gillian at the water break. "It's all over me but I'm not cooling down. It just sits there." Gillian wiped her dripping forehead with her wrist. "Mine too. It evaporates, doesn't it? That's the whole point of sweating. My grandmother says that." Jade looked at her soaked sleeve, then at the gray, heavy sky. "Not today. Today it just stays wet."

She tested it the only way she could. She grabbed a paper towel from the bench, soaked it in her water bottle, and hung it over the fence. Then she dried her other towel completely and hung that one beside it. When Coach called them back, she checked both. The wet towel was still soaked. The damp one had barely shrunk.

"That's it," she told Philemon at the fence. "The air's too humid. Sweat evaporates slower, so we're overheating out here without even knowing it." Philemon, who privately envied Gillian her starting spot and wanted more than anything to keep his own, frowned. "So the heat isn't the problem. The stickiness is."

Coach overheard, and by the next muggy practice he had shortened the drills and made water breaks a privilege nobody had to earn, which some parents called controversial. Jade just grinned and pointed at the fence, where her two towels still hung like evidence. "See for yourself," she said.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Adding the tops and the bottoms separately gives a wrong answer: one half plus one third is five sixths, not two fifths.
story:
The clock above the study table showed 3:40, and Sophia still had three fraction problems left before her mom picked her up. She flattened her notebook page and stared at the first one: one half plus one third. Across the table, her classmate Penelope was supposed to be reading for a book report, but she kept peeking over her novel.

"Two fifths," said a boy at the next table, sliding his paper toward Alyson. "One half plus one third. You just add the tops and the bottoms."

Alyson frowned at it. "Wait. You started with a half. Now your answer is smaller than the half you started with. How does adding a third make your piece shrink?"

The boy grabbed his pencil and drew two pizzas, shading the pieces. He sat back, then exhaled slowly through his nose. "Two fifths is less than one half," he admitted. "So that can't be right."

Sophia copied his pizza idea onto her own paper. She drew her half, then drew the third next to it, then sliced both pizzas into the same number of pieces so the slices matched. When she counted them, her pencil hovered. "Five sixths," she said, a little too loudly for the library. The boy and Alyson both turned. She held up her drawings. "If you cut everything into sixths, a half is three sixths and a third is two sixths. Three plus two is five. Five sixths."

"You fixed my diagnosis of the problem," the boy said, tapping his erased two fifths. "I thought fractions were trivial. Clearly they are not."

Mr. Reddy, the librarian, appeared with his cart of returns and raised one eyebrow at their volume. Sophia mouthed "sorry" and bent over her next problem: one half minus one third. Same pizzas, same sixths. Three sixths minus two sixths. She wrote her answer and slid the paper toward Penelope.

"One sixth," Penelope read, and gave her a quiet thumbs-up. Sophia grinned and flipped to the last problem.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
Alexa noticed it before they even left the airport: the sealed bag of chips she'd bought in Denver was as tight as a balloon, swollen and firm in her backpack. She hadn't opened it on the plane because she'd been saving it for the beach, and now, standing on the warm sand while her dad hauled the cooler down the path, she squeezed the bag and frowned. Nothing had leaked. Nothing had been opened. She pressed a fresh bag her dad had bought at the shop by the boardwalk, and it gave easily, slack and soft. Same brand, same size. So something had happened to hers between home and here.

She sat on the towel and texted Catalina, who loved this kind of puzzle.

"You know how my chips bag got all puffy on the flight? The new one here is soft. Same chips! What changed?"

Catalina's reply came while Alexa was tracing shapes in the sand with her toe. "My dad flies for work. He says the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level. Look it up if you don't believe me."

Alexa did look it up, shading the screen with her hand. The words matched Catalina's text exactly. So the bag had been sealed at home, close to sea level, and then it had ridden for hours in air as thin as a mountaintop's. The bag had puffed up like that because of where it had been, not because of anything inside it. She would have to revise her first guess, which had been that a baggage handler had squashed it. The opposite of squashing had happened.

To test it, she carried the puffed bag down to the water's edge and held it under the surface, watching it strain against her palms like some extravagant air-filled organism trying to rise. Mr. Lau from next door was setting up an umbrella a few yards away, and he waved.

"That looks ready to pop," he called.

"That's the whole point," Alexa said, and let it go.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
Quinn deleted the photo exactly ten minutes after she posted it. Ten minutes felt like a fair trade: long enough for her friends to see her wearing the clown-nose filter with a caption in all caps, short enough that the whole internet would never know. She sat at the kitchen computer that evening, playing a game of Monopoly against herself while her mom cooked, and almost forgot about it.

The next morning, the photo was in the class group chat. Mackenna had sent it with three crying-laughing faces. Quinn stared at the screen so long the monitor's power-saving dim kicked in. She hadn't sent it to Mackenna. She hadn't sent it to anyone. Her page showed nothing, just her careful pictures of the cat and the science fair ribbon. She clicked her own profile twice, scrolling, hunting for the clown nose like it might be hiding between the good posts.

"Where did you get that?" she typed to Mackenna.

"I saved it last night," Mackenna wrote back. "Before you deleted it. It was too funny to lose."

Quinn leaned back. So deleting hadn't done what she thought it did. Deleting took the photo off her page, sure, but it couldn't climb into Mackenna's phone and take the copy back. Anything saved or screenshotted stayed saved, like a letter already mailed. She tested it in her head: what if Claira had saved it too? What if a stranger had? She looked at the photo again, at her own front porch visible in the background, the house number just readable. Who had seen that number?

She thought about asking her mom to help, but the words would have to precede the photo itself, and she wasn't ready for that yet. Besides, she wanted to fix it her own way first.

"Delete it from the chat," she typed to Mackenna. "Please."

Mackenna replied with a single thumbs-up, and then, after a pause, one more message: "Okay. But copy something of mine sometime, and we're even."

Quinn saved Mackenna's message, then sat very still with her hand on the mouse, listening to her mom hum over the sound of the frying pan.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
story:
Edouard spread his rock collection across the kitchen table, twenty-three stones lined up in a wobbly row. His science homework said he had to sort them into three piles: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic, by how they were formed. Igneous came from cooled magma, sedimentary from pressed-down layers, and metamorphic from rock that heat and pressure had squeezed and changed. He could identify most of them by their look, the glassy black one that had surely cooled from something molten, the layered tan one with stripes like a sandwich.

The problem was the fossil. His friend Harman had given him a note in class that morning, folded into a paper football: "My cousin found a fossil in her creek and everyone at school saw it. I want one for the project. Bring your best rocks Saturday and we'll crack them open. H." Edouard envied Harman's cousin her fossil, a little spiral shell printed right in the stone, and he wanted to find one for his friend. He looked down the row and picked out the most promising candidates: a chunk of gray metamorphic schist, a piece of dark igneous basalt, and a slab of layered limestone.

Then he stopped. He thought about the shell in the picture, how perfect and whole it was. That limestone had stripes, one layer on top of another, like pages. Layers meant sedimentary. And a shell trapped in the layers would get pressed into stone along with everything else. He imagined the basalt instead, cooling from something hot, and the schist baking and squeezing until its minerals rearranged themselves. A shell wouldn't survive that. Fossils had to be in the layered stuff, almost always, because the heat that made the other two kinds of rock destroyed any remains. The whole point of a fossil was that something had survived.

He tested his idea. From the garage he brought the hammer and an old towel and cracked open a piece of the limestone, carefully, wearing his dad's safety glasses. Inside were two faint ridges, like the edge of an ancient ripple. He texted a photo to his cousin, and she wrote back, "That's a ripple mark! Sedimentary. Bring it Saturday." He sat back and grinned at the irony of it: Harman had been hunting fossils for weeks in the creek gravel, kicking past the layered stones because they looked boring, while hauling home shiny volcanic pebbles that could never hold anything.

Edouard wrote his reply: "Stop checking the dark rocks. Fossils are almost only in sedimentary rock. The heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains. Come over, my mom made cookies." Outside the window a nocturnal raccoon was already padding along the fence, and somewhere in that dark yard, layered stones waited. "Bring a bag," he added. "We're going hunting."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
Andrew had been waiting for this moment since roughly the third grade, and now that it had arrived, the phone store smelled suspiciously like carpet cleaner and disappointment. His father had one rule: "I supervise the first month. Every app, every download." Andrew nodded the way you nod when the other option is walking out with nothing.

The clerk handed over a sleek blue phone, and Andrew's friend Lyla had already texted him three times from across town, or at least she said she had. Her messages weren't arriving. Nothing was arriving. He refreshed the inbox, held the phone toward the ceiling like it might catch a better signal, and even restarted it twice, because restarting things was what his father did to the Wi-Fi router and it worked about forty percent of the time.

Then he noticed a tiny airplane in the corner of the screen. The clerk had turned something on while setting it up. "Airplane mode," the clerk said when Andrew pointed at it. Andrew thought about that. If it was named after airplanes, it probably had something to do with flying, and on airplanes you had to turn off your signals. Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts. So the phone wasn't broken. It was just sitting there in polite radio silence, ignoring Lyla entirely.

He tapped the airplane off. The screen buzzed. Three texts from Lyla appeared at once, then a fourth: "Did you die?"

"Almost," Andrew typed back. His father leaned over the counter, peering at the screen with the concentration of a man inspecting a monsoon forecast, and outside the window the parking lot shimmered with heat, fertile ground for every dropped call in the county.

"One month of supervision," his father said.

"Thirty days," Andrew agreed. "Not one more."

The phone buzzed again. Lyla had sent a picture of her cat wearing sunglasses.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
Hunter counted the elevator buttons twice, because the first count had to be wrong. Three, then five, then six, all the way to twelve. There was no four. He was visiting Reyansh's apartment for the first time, holding a box of mangoes his mom had sent as a gift, and they had exactly fifteen minutes to get upstairs before Reyansh's grandmother served dinner at six o'clock.

"You're staring at the buttons," Reyansh said, jabbing the seven. "My cousin did the same thing when he visited. In Chinese, the word for four sounds a lot like the word for death, so some buildings in East Asia just skip the fourth floor." Hunter filed that away, amazed, as the doors closed.

In the humming elevator he remembered last summer, when his family drove two hours so he could bow to his great-aunt and accept a red envelope with both hands. His mom had drilled him for a week beforehand: shoes off at the door, no pointing, wait for the eldest person to lift their chopsticks first. He had been terrified of getting it wrong, but the great-aunt had grinned at him and called him a polite young man, and afterward they ate noodles so spicy his nose ran.

At Reyansh's door, Hunter hesitated, then handed over the mangoes with both hands, the way he had been taught. Reyansh's grandmother took them the same way and pressed her palms together. "Come, come, dinner is almost ready."

The table was already set. Hunter noticed that everyone waited while the grandmother sat, so he stayed standing too, holding his chair, until Reyansh nudged him and whispered, "She'll serve the rice first." Steam curled off the bowls, and the smell of ginger filled the small kitchen. The grandmother scooped a mountain of rice into Hunter's bowl, far more than anyone else's, and he understood that the extra portion, exactly proportional to how far he had traveled, was a kind of welcome he could eat.

"The elevator still has no four," he said, to nobody in particular.

"Never has," said Reyansh's grandmother, and ladled him more rice.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Alice pressed her palm against the mixing bowl and frowned. The dough inside sat flat and dense as clay, though Ms. Hassan's recipe had promised it would double in an hour. Across the community kitchen, Harmony was shaping her own dough into a smooth round ball, and hers had already puffed up over the rim of its bowl like a rising moon.

"What did you do differently?" Alice asked, coming over to assess both bowls side by side. Same flour, same spoon, same warm corner by the oven.

Harmony shrugged. "I just mixed it like it said."

Alice walked back to her station and looked at the sink where she'd filled her measuring cup. She had been in a hurry, so she'd turned the tap to hot. The water had steamed against the cold cup. She thought about the little granules of yeast she'd stirred in, so small you couldn't watch what happened to them. Yeast feeds on the sugars in dough, her older sister liked to say, and releases carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles. That's why bread rises. But could the yeast have been hurt before it ever got the chance to eat?

She had a simple way to find out. She spooned a pinch of fresh yeast into two cups of water, one lukewarm, one hot from the tap, and set them on the windowsill. Ten minutes later the lukewarm cup had grown a foamy tan head, like a tiny parliament of bubbles holding a meeting. The hot cup sat still and clear.

"My water was too hot," Alice said, mostly to herself. "I killed it."

"So the bread machine isn't obsolete after all," Harmony called over. "You just have to be nicer to the yeast."

Alice scraped the dead dough into the compost bin and started again, this time testing the water against her wrist the way her grandmother did with a baby's bottle. When the new dough went into its bowl, she leaned down close and whispered, "Eat well, little guys."

Harmony laughed so hard she dropped her flour scoop.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Westminster-style legislatures such as Canada's and the United Kingdom's, first reading introduces a bill and has it printed without debate.
story:
The community centre's craft room smelled like glue and old coffee, and every table had been pushed aside except one long one draped with a green bedsheet. Mr. Almeida had set up a screen at the front to show the legislature channel, and Kenzi kept glancing at the clock because she wanted to finish early enough to claim the good basketball before open gym filled up.

"Today we run our own legislature," Mr. Almeida said. "Ella, you're the government member introducing the bill about the skateboard ramp in Riverside Park."

Ella stood up with her notes, ready for a fight. She had practised her speech twice on the bus, ready for arguments, ready for anything. She read the title out loud, and then nothing happened. Nobody stood up to argue. Nobody even raised a hand. She stood there holding her papers while the clerk, played by Lucas, wrote the title in a big notebook and slid a printed copy down the table.

"That's it?" she asked. "I prepared a whole speech."

On the screen behind them, the real legislature was doing the exact same thing. A member said a bill's title, the Speaker said a few words, and the item passed in seconds. No speeches, no debate. Ella watched, frowning, and then looked at her own printed copy sitting on the bedsheet.

"It's the first reading," Lucas said, not looking up from his notebook. "The bill gets introduced and printed, and that's all."

Ella sat down slowly. So the arguing came later, at some other reading, and this part existed just to put the words on paper. A bill could transform from one line in a notebook into an actual park ramp, but only by climbing through every step in order, and the first step was the quiet one. She flipped her speech over and started writing a plan for the debate that would come next.

Kenzi leaned over. "Can we speed this up?"

"Second reading now," Ella announced. "And I have questions for the rebellious member who keeps voting against ramps."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A callback closing returns to the opening hook at the end, which makes a speech feel complete.
story:
Emile stood outside Room 4B with his speech cards sweating in his hand, and the problem was simple: he had no ending. He had a hook about his grandmother's parrot, who screamed "Fire!" at breakfast every morning, and he had three points about false alarms wasting rescue crews. But his last card just said "conclusion?" with a question mark he had drawn himself, as if the paper might answer.

Tayla bounced over and read his cards upside down, a talent she was annoyingly proud of. "You can't go in there with a question mark where your ending goes. Mr. Delgado will make that face." She simulated Mr. Delgado's face: one eyebrow up, one eyebrow down, mouth a flat line of disappointment. Emile laughed even though his stomach did not.

Before he could argue, a folded note landed on his shoe. It was from Raymond, who was leaning against the water fountain ten feet away, grinning like a villain in a movie with a synthetic shark. The note read: "Dear protagonist of Room 4B. Your parrot opened your speech. Guess who closes it? PS you owe me a pretzel. PPS a callback closing returns to the opening hook at the end. It makes a speech feel complete. Raymond."

Emile stared at the note. He had been trying to invent a brand-new ending, some grand sentence he didn't have, when the answer had been sitting in his first line the whole time. He flipped through his points in his head and found the spot: after the third point about rescue crews, the parrot could come back. "That's the callback closing," he told Tayla, tapping the note. "The parrot opens it, the parrot closes it." He scribbled on his last card: the parret learns to yell it only when it's real.

"You owe Raymond a pretzel either way," Tayla said. "Both ways, actually. He told me you'd say that."

Inside Room 4B, Emile got his two minutes. His voice wobbled on the first sentence, steadied on the second, and held through all three points, because he kept glancing at the parrot card like it was a friend in the audience. At the end, he put the cards down. "Maybe the lesson isn't to ignore the parrot," he said. "Maybe the lesson is to teach the parrot. And when Grandma finally did, the whole kitchen cheered, and the bird, delighted, screamed 'Fire!' one last time, just to hear everyone cheer again."

The judge circled something on her sheet. In the hallway afterward, Raymond held out his hand, palm up. "One pretzel. Synthetic ones not accepted."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text.
story:
Keira stared at her notes so hard the words went blurry. Mr. Leung had written one comment at the top of her draft: "Theme needs a quotation to prove it." Her theme, she was sure, was that home is something you build, not something you find. The problem was the only good quote in chapter nine, and it said, "He kept the key around his neck even after they lost the house." Which "he"? The book had two brothers, Ravi and Tomas, plus a landlord with a walking stick, and honestly any of the three could have carried a key.

"Give it up," said Felicia, sliding into the next seat with her own draft, already three paragraphs longer than anyone else's. Felicia's secret goal was to finish first so she could read her horse magazines under the desk. "Just write 'he' and hope Mr. Leung is sleepy when he marks it."

"He's never sleepy. He once corrected a comma in my margin note." Keira flipped to the MLA pages at the back of the class anthology, hunting for something about pronouns, and stopped. There it was, in small print under a sample quote: brackets around the word "she," where the original had said "she." No, wait, she read it again. In the original text the word had just been a pronoun, and the student writer had swapped in the character's name inside square brackets.

"So that's what those are for," she said aloud. "Square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, in MLA style." She grabbed her pen and wrote: "He [Tomas] kept the key around his neck even after they lost the house." Now the quote proved her theme, because Tomas, the brother who moved four times in one year, was the one who persevered.

Felicia peered over, sighed, and pushed her horse magazines back into her bag. "Great. Now I have to add a quote too, or you'll beat me."

Keira grinned. "You could always write about the landlord. He's my favourite tenant in the whole book, even though he technically owns it."

"That's not what tenant means, and you know it."

"Then hurry up and prove it," Keira said, and slid the anthology across the desk.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Practicing a speech out loud with a timer matters because reading silently is faster than speaking, so a speech often runs longer than expected.
story:
Clara had her speech about the class petition written out on index cards, and it looked short. Two minutes was nothing. She read the cards silently, moving her lips, and figured she had plenty of room, so she added a joke and an extra point about how fertile the school garden would be if they got a longer recess to tend it.

"Let's time it," she said, dialing Denis on the kitchen phone. "You be the timer."

"Ready," said Denis, who wanted the joke in the speech kept in no matter what, because he had written it. "Actually wait, I want the joke kept in no matter what."

"That's the deal." Clara clicked the stopwatch on the counter, stood up straight the way she planned to stand in front of Ms. Almeida's class, and started speaking out loud. "Did you know that eleven students can change a whole school? That's how many names are on our petition." She went on. Point one, point two, then the joke, then the garden part, and she was just warming up to her point about how the principal's grandmother deserved a pension and a nice long rest after thirty years of teaching, when Denis yelled, "Two minutes!"

Clara stopped mid-sentence. "What? No. It's short. I read the whole thing in like a minute."

"I'm telling you, the stopwatch says two minutes and five seconds, and you weren't even done," Denis said. "That thing is a monster."

Clara stared at the cards. She read them silently again, watching the clock. Fifty-two seconds. Then she read them out loud. Two minutes and five seconds, easy, and that was without pausing to breathe or waiting for laughs. Something was going on that she couldn't see on the paper. Reading silently was faster than speaking, so the speech that looked short was actually long, and it ran longer out loud than she ever would have guessed. That was the hidden trap, and now she knew it was there.

"So we cut the joke," she said.

"So we cut your grandma pension thing," said Denis.

They argued for ten seconds, then Clara grabbed a pencil. "We cut both, and I practice out loud with the timer every single time, because paper lies." She stood up, clicked the stopwatch, and began, "Did you know that eleven students can change a whole school?"

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: A top, or apex, predator is at the end of its food chain and, as an adult, has no natural predators of its own.
story:
Alexandre spread his poster board on the picnic table and weighted the corners with rocks, because the afternoon breeze had already flipped it twice. He was supposed to draw a food chain for science homework, starting with the sun and ending with a top predator, and then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. He had the sun. He had grass. After that, the chain dissolved into an argument he could not stop replaying.

At the science museum yesterday, Rosalie had stood in front of the raptor display and insisted that the hawk was at the top of the chain in their local woods. Landyn had laughed and said it was the owl, obviously. They had looked at Alexandre, and he had shrugged, and the moment had slid away into the gift shop. He kept thinking about that shrug. Rosalie had seemed annoyed all the way home.

Now he sharpened his pencil and started over. Sun, arrow, grass, arrow, a grasshopper he made lumpy on purpose so it looked real, arrow, a mouse, arrow. He paused at the last box. Hawk or owl? He wrote HAWK in big letters, then sat staring at it. Something Ms. Zhu had said when he'd watered her tomatoes last week drifted back to him. "The hawk in my yard," she'd said, tapping the fence, "nobody hunts that hawk. She hunts everyone else." He had not understood why that mattered until this exact moment at the picnic table.

If nothing hunts the hawk, then the hawk ends the chain. It's not just the biggest or the scariest, it's the end. "Apex," he said out loud, remembering the word from a museum label. He wrote it under HAWK and drew a bold line, like a wall, after the box. Nothing came after.

His little brother's laser pointer, borrowed without asking, sat in Alexandre's pocket. He used it to trace the arrows one by one, red dot sliding from sun to grass to grasshopper to mouse to hawk, then bumping against the wall he'd drawn. Then he did the experiment part of his brain had been begging for. He covered the mouse with his hand. Chain: sun, grass, grasshopper, wall. The hawk box floated there with nothing leading into it. He imagined the woods in a year where all the mice were gone. The hawk would starve or move away, and then, with nothing eating them, the grasshoppers would multiply until the turbulent little swarms chewed the grass down to dirt.

He pulled his hand away and the mouse came back, and the whole chain snapped together again, like it had been waiting.

The gate creaked. Rosalie stood there holding her own blank poster board. "My mom said you were out here," she said. "Also, I looked it up. Owl or hawk, either one works. As an adult, nothing hunts them. They're the end of the chain."

Alexandre slid over on the bench and tapped the empty space beside his hawk wall. "Then demonstrate it. Draw yours next to mine."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: An oven setting of 350 degrees Fahrenheit is about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius.
story:
Grace had been begging to run the Saturday baking station at the community kitchen all month, and finally she and Ms. Moretti had reached a negotiation: Grace could bake the muffins alone if Ms. Moretti stayed nearby for emergencies only. Now she stood in front of the big steel oven, recipe printed from an American website, feeling like a scientist on launch day. Zendaya and Katerina had petitioned to be her official taste-testers, and they leaned over the counter like judges at a contest.

"Step one, preheat the oven," Grace read out loud. "Three hundred fifty degrees." She spun the dial and stopped. The oven's display showed only Celsius numbers, going up to 250. A cold little knot formed in her stomach. The recipe wanted a number her oven couldn't even show. "It's broken," Katerina said. "Or obsolete," said Zendaya. "This oven is older than my grandmother's radio."

Grace was about to panic when she remembered the thermometer poster in Ms. Moretti's classroom last year. The class had compared weather in Chicago and Rome on the same day, and Grace had noticed that the same warmth got two different numbers depending on the country. American recipes used Fahrenheit; most ovens everywhere else used Celsius. That meant 350 on the recipe wasn't impossible, it was just written in the other system. Somewhere on her oven's scale there had to be a matching number, and she had a hunch about how to find it.

She grabbed the old cookbook from the shelf above the sink, the one printed in Italy, and flipped until she found a muffin recipe that looked nearly identical, same flour, same butter, same baking time of twenty minutes. She put the two recipes side by side. The Italian one said 180 degrees. The American one said 350. Same muffins, same time, same result, so 350 degrees Fahrenheit had to be about the same heat as 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. She dialed the oven to 180 and pressed start, and the red light blinked on like a tiny victory.

While the oven heated, the three of them measured flour, cracked eggs, and argued about whether to fold in blueberries or chocolate chips. Zendaya won the argument by promising to wash every bowl. The batter went into twelve paper cups, and Grace slid the tray in at exactly the number she had reasoned out. For twenty minutes she watched through the glass as the muffins rose into golden domes, and when she pulled the tray out, the kitchen smelled like a bakery.

Katerina bit into the first muffin, still steaming. "Grace," she said, "petition granted. You are officially the muffin queen of Saturdays."

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: In an ordered pair like (3, 5), the first number tells how far to move across along the x-axis and the second tells how far to move up or down.
story:
Hailey spread the graph paper across the kitchen table and set a bowl of popcorn between Stefan and Noam. They were playing coordinate battleship, the game Ms. Esposito had shown the class on Friday, and each of them had three hidden ships drawn on a secret grid.

"I'm calling D, and I'm firing at (3, 5)," Noam announced, pointing at Hailey's grid with a popcorn kernel.

Hailey counted up from the bottom corner. "Miss." She marked the shot with a small x and slid the paper toward Stefan so he could verify.

Stefan frowned. "Wait. You counted wrong. You went up three and across five."

"Because that's what (3, 5) means," Hailey said. "The three comes first, so it's the up part."

Noam shook his head. "That's backwards. My brother says the first number is the across one." Hailey looked at her grid. If Noam was right, then her whole strategy was ruined, because she had been reading every ordered pair the same wrong way. She thought about the homework spread beside her, a page of two-step equations she was supposed to plot as lines. If she had solved for x and then moved the wrong direction, every point on her line would land in the wrong place, and the line would be a mirror of itself.

She pulled out her phone and searched the rule. There it was: in an ordered pair like (3, 5), the first number tells how far to move across along the x-axis and the second tells how far to move up or down. She read it twice. "You were right," she told Noam. "Across first, then up. I've been doing it backwards the whole game."

"So that shot," Noam said slowly, "might have been a hit."

Stefan traced it on Hailey's grid with his finger, across three along the x-axis and up five. His finger landed on the wing of her battleship. "Hit," Hailey admitted, and Noam did a small victory spin that knocked over the popcorn.

After he and Stefan went home, Hailey stayed at the table with her equation page and a fresh sheet. She solved the first one, 2x plus 1 equals 7, and got x equals 3. Then she picked a second value, worked out the pair, and plotted it slowly: across first, then up. She added a second point, then a third, and connected them. The line ran exactly where it should, clean and straight across the grid.

She held the page up to the kitchen light, then found her little sister in the hallway and said, "Come here, I'll teach you the across-then-up rule. First one to sink my battleship wins."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: In Python, input() always returns text, even when the user types digits, so the answer must be converted with int() before it can be multiplied as a number.
story:
David spun his chair toward the laptop in Simran's basement, where the old couch smelled like popcorn and the lamp made a warm circle of light on the table. Simran had promised to teach him a real program today, not just print statements, and she wasn't going to let him give up early. "You wanted the times table for any number," she said, sliding the keyboard toward him. "So ask for one."

David typed the program while Ayoub leaned over his shoulder, munching chips. He wrote a line that asked for a number, then a loop that counted from one to twelve and multiplied. When he ran it and typed 7, the screen filled up with nonsense, rows and rows of strange repeated text instead of 7, 14, 21. "It's broken," Ayoub said, reaching for the keyboard. "Let me restart the whole thing."

"Wait," David said. He pivoted the chair away from Ayoub's grab and studied the screen. The output wasn't random; it was the seven written out again and again, mushed together. He narrowed his eyes. It was like the program didn't think the 7 was a number at all. "Simran," he said slowly, "what comes back from input?" She just raised an eyebrow, conserving her hints the way she always did until he'd tried something first. David tested a tiny idea: he typed print(input()) and then print(input() + input()), entered 7 both times, and got 77 instead of 14. There it was. "Input always gives you text," he said, "even when you type digits. So I have to convert it with int before I can multiply it."

He added the conversion, saved, and ran it again. This time, typing 7 gave him 7, 14, 21, all the way up to 84, clean as anything. Ayoub, who had been shaking his head the whole time, stopped and grinned. "Okay, I changed my mind, that's actually cool. Do mine, do the nines." David cracked his knuckles and typed 9 at the blinking cursor.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
story:
The sanctuary smelled of old wood and honey cake from the table nobody would touch until sundown. Romy had fasted until lunch before, but this year she wanted the whole day, all the way to the stars, because her mother said that was what made it feel real. By the time the afternoon service began, her stomach had stopped growling and started whispering, and she pressed her prayer book against it like a shield.

During the reading she saw her cousin Luc slip out to the hallway, and he was walking the way people walk on a boat, one hand on the wall. Luc was twelve and had diabetes, and Romy knew what the small case in his pocket was for. But today was Yom Kippur, and eating on Yom Kippur felt like the one thing you could never do. Would drinking juice violate the fast? she wondered. Surely it did. She followed him anyway, just to make sure he didn't fall.

In the hallway Luc sat on the bench and handed her a folded note, the kind their grandmother used to send. "Read it," he said. "My hands are shaky." The note was from the rabbi, written that morning in his slanted handwriting. "Luc, your health comes first. Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger. In that case a person is not merely allowed to eat or drink. A person is required to." Romy read it twice. Required. It was the opposite of what she had guessed, like a door that pushed when you pulled.

She dug the juice box out of his case, stabbed the straw through the foil, and held it steady while he drank. "The rabbi says you have to," she said, "so don't argue." Luc laughed, which turned into a cough, and then his hands went still.

Romy walked back into the sanctuary holding the empty juice box. Her own stomach whispered again, louder, but she was not dizzy like Luc had been, only hungry, which was different. She dropped the juice box in the bin by the door and took her seat next to her mother, who leaned over and whispered, "Everything all right?"

"Luc had to drink something," Romy whispered back. "It's the rule."

Her mother looked at her for a moment, then nodded and put one arm along the back of the pew. The cantor's voice rose, aggressive and beautiful at the same time, filling the room like water filling a glass. Romy closed her eyes. Maybe the fast was a metaphor, she thought, a way of remembering, and remembering did not mean you had to hurt. When the singing ended, she opened her eyes and found the right page on her own.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
story:
The bathroom mirror still showed the bangs Anna had cut herself six days ago, crooked on the left, and every time she looked at them she felt the same hot prickle in her ears. She had known even then, with the scissors in her hand, that it was a bad idea, and she had done it anyway. On her bed lay a book her mom had brought home from a colleague at work, a thick one about the teenage brain, and Anna had opened it mostly out of boredom while her hair air-dried.

One page stopped her. It said the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. She read the sentence twice. So the part of her that was supposed to stop her from doing dumb things was literally unfinished, like a bridge with the last span still missing. She didn't want to use it as an excuse, though. She wanted to find out whether waiting could do the job her brain hadn't built yet.

That afternoon Guneet called, excited about her balcony tomato project. "The bees finally came to pollinate the flowers," Guneet said. "Two actual bees. If the tomatoes set fruit, I'm entering the science fair, and Rachel says she'll help with the poster." Then Guneet's voice dropped. "Some kids in the group chat are saying my pots look toxic, like the spray paint is poisoning everything. It's not, I checked. I want to quit the chat."

"Don't quit," Anna said. "Wait ten minutes first." She told her about the prefrontal cortex, the unfinished part in charge of impulses, and how she'd been testing it herself since the bangs: whenever she wanted to do something fast, she wrote it down and waited. Her test list already had three crossed-out items on it, including a snappy reply to Rachel about a borrowed hoodie.

"Fine," Guneet said. "Ten minutes. Starting now."

Anna set the kitchen timer, and they sat on the floor counting the tomatoes in the seed catalogue until it rang.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement; unlike a judge, a mediator does not decide who is right.
story:
Anis's garage smelled like glue and burnt toast, and the pollinator robot sat in the middle of the workbench like a small metal bee. "It's my idea," Anis said, arms crossed. "I said a robot could pollinate the tomatoes with a cotton swab." Katherine jabbed a finger at her sketchbook. "But the design is mine. Every bracket, every wire." They both turned to Luca at the same time. "You decide," Anis said. "Tell us whose robot it is."

Luca felt the weight of it, like being handed the last slice of pizza while two people watched. "Okay," he said, and pointed at Katherine's sketches. "Designs matter more, so it's mostly yours." Anis's face went stormy and he snatched the screwdriver. Katherine flipped her sketchbook shut. Luca tried again, saying maybe it was mostly Anis's, and now Katherine was the stormy one. The robot sat untouched while its two builders sat on opposite crates.

Luca carried a jar of bolts outside to cool off and found Ms. Sato from next door watering her peppers. He told her the whole mess. "A mediator doesn't decide who's right," she said, squeezing her hose off. "A judge does that. A mediator helps two sides reach their own agreement." She went back to her peppers, but Luca ran the words over in his head all the way back across the driveway.

In the garage he set the jar down. "New plan. I'm not the judge. I'm the mediator. That means you two make the deal, and I just help." Anis squinted. "So who wins?"
