"Nobody announces a winner," Luca said. "Just tell each other what you actually want." Anis went first, quieter now. "Credit for the idea." Katherine shrugged. "Credit for the build." They looked at each other, and Katherine opened her sketchbook again and wrote at the top, Pollinator 1, idea by Anis, build by Katherine. "Draw it on the robot too," Anis said, already grinning.

Luca picked up the robot to celebrate and froze. Greenish crust was creeping across the battery contacts. "Leaked batteries," he said. "That stuff is corrosive, we have to clean it off before it eats the terminals." Anis grabbed the baking soda and Katherine fetched the little brushes, and all three of them leaned over the bench as the powder fizzed softly against the crust. "One minute to liftoff," Anis announced. "Somebody open the door for the bees."

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, a 'repeat 10' block runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, while a 'forever' block keeps going until the program is stopped.
story:
Carson had claimed the computer in the back corner of the public library, the one next to the window, so he could see the parking lot where his mom would pull in. His game was almost done. A little purple monster was supposed to chase the player's cat around the screen, and every time the cat dodged, the score went up by one.

"Watch this," he said as Liliane dropped into the chair beside him. He clicked the green flag. The monster marched toward the cat, quick and hungry, and then, halfway across the stage, it stopped. Frozen. Staring at nothing like a statue of a very disappointed monster. Liliane laughed so hard she had to set down her stack of books before she dropped them.

"That is the saddest villain I have ever seen," she said. "He just gives up."

"He doesn't give up, something's wrong," Carson said. He bent close to the screen and traced the blocks with his finger. Under the green flag sat a repeat 10 block, with "move 10 steps" tucked inside it. He sat back. Repeat 10 runs whatever is inside exactly ten times, he thought, so the monster takes ten steps and then quits, like a wind-up toy with nowhere left to wind. His eyes slid to the menu of blocks, where the forever block waited like it had been patient the whole time. Forever keeps going until the program is stopped. He swapped repeat 10 for forever, and this time the monster charged across the screen and kept charging, wobbling after the cat like it would never, ever stop.

"Terrifying," Liliane said. "Now illustrate the danger by letting the monster catch me once." She grabbed the mouse and steered the cat straight into its path. The score flipped to zero and the word CAUGHT flashed in enormous letters. Liliane sneezed. "Great, and now I'm getting an infection on top of humiliation."

"Ms. Sánchez would say I'm an impartial judge," Carson said, restarting the game. "I let the cat win AND the monster win. Everybody gets a trophy." Liliane shoved his shoulder, and the monster came wobbling after the cat again.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat.
story:
Rosalie sat on her grandmother's porch steps with Lucille and Jade, all three of them still damp from a soccer game in the August heat. Lucille peeled off her shin guard and held it at arm's length like it had insulted her.

"That is the worst smell in the history of smells," Lucille announced. "Sweat is disgusting."

"Fresh sweat has almost no smell," Rosalie said. "It's true. The smell comes from bacteria on your skin breaking down the sweat."

Jade sniffed her own forearm, then wished she hadn't. "Then why does my arm smell like a locker room that lost a fight?"

"Because the sweat has been sitting there for a while," Rosalie said. "The bacteria had time to work on it. Like milk turning." Lucille made a gagging noise that made the neighbor's cat leave the yard.

Rosalie had learned this from a book her grandmother kept in the bathroom, and she wanted to prove it. So she marched inside, filled the kitchen sink, and submerged a clean washcloth while her grandmother raised one eyebrow but said nothing. "New sweat test," Rosalie declared, wringing it out. "I'm going to rinse the sweat off right away. Watch."

She wiped her arms and the back of her neck with the warm, wet cloth, then scrubbed with soap, then dared Lucille to sniff. Lucille inhaled like a judge at a pie contest. "Nothing. You smell like... grandma's soap."

"Exactly," Rosalie said, feeling as triumphant as any protagonist in any book ever written. "Bacteria gone, smell gone."

"You should be more assertive about this," Jade said. "Tell the whole team. Half of them think sweat itself stinks, and the other half are the reason the bus smells."

Her grandmother appeared in the doorway with three clean towels and a bar of deodorant still in its wrapper. "Showers," she said, pointing up the stairs. "All three. And Rosalie, you're buying the deodorant next time."

Rosalie grabbed the towel and led the charge up the stairs, Lucille arguing the whole way that her shin guard was still the true villain.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final.
story:
The stadium was already roaring when Tristan found his seat between his dad and Gordon, and the warm-up hadn't even finished. "Best tickets I've ever touched," Gordon said, holding his up to the lights like it was made of gold. Tristan's little brother leaned across Dad to argue about who would win, and that's when the real fight started.

"Argentina," Dad said firmly. "They won the first World Cup. My father told me a hundred times."

"Grandpa is wrong," Tristan's brother shouted over the crowd. "It was Uruguay."

Dad laughed, but he didn't look like he was joking. "You're going to tell me about my own heritage? Uruguay wasn't even in it, I bet."

Tristan's stomach did a small flip, the kind he got before a penalty kick. Dad hated being wrong, and if the argument kept going, the whole first half would be ruined. He thought about what he actually knew. Somewhere in his memory was a page from a project he'd done in Ms. Hosseini's class, a list of winners. He couldn't see the page directly, but he remembered drawing a small flag next to the very first entry, and the flag had a sun in the corner. Argentina's flag had a sun too, which was probably why Dad was mixed up. But the page had said Uruguay. He was almost sure.

"Wait," Tristan said, and pulled out his phone. "Cash said we could use his hotspot if we needed anything today." He searched first World Cup winner and read the screen twice before saying anything, because being wrong himself would be worse than staying quiet.

"Uruguay," he said. "The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final."

Dad stared at the screen. Tristan braced for an argument, but instead Dad rubbed his chin and grinned. "Four to two. So it was close, at least. My father would have fainted." He turned to Tristan's brother and held out his hand. "You win this one."

The whistle blew, the players accelerated down the pitch, and the whole family rose shouting together. "Next argument," Gordon yelled over the noise, "I'm looking everything up before anyone speaks."

"Not before the second half," Tristan said, eyes on the ball.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: APR stands for annual percentage rate, the yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow.
story:
Ariana counted the bills in her pocket for the third time: eleven dollars. The jam vendor at the farmers' market sold small jars of her favorite sour cherry preserve for eight dollars, but the big jar, the one that would last all winter, cost twenty-two. She had been walking past that booth for four Saturdays, and each week the big jars got fewer. Today only five were left.

Her grandfather had let her look at a credit card offer that came in his mail, and one part had stuck in her head. "APR," she said to Zaiden, who was leaning on the table beside her, eyeing honey sticks. "That's on the card offer Grandpa got. APR stands for annual percentage rate. It's the yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow." Zaiden nodded slowly, like he was filing that away, which he probably was, since he kept a notebook of facts about sharks.

"So if I borrowed the money," Ariana said, "I'd be paying extra, every year, on top of what I owe." She tried to imagine the eleven missing dollars turning into more than eleven, the invisible cost stacking up like pennies in a jar she couldn't see. She wanted to test it. Mr. Visver, who sold honey two booths down and let kids help him stack jars on Saturdays, sometimes paid her five dollars for an hour of work.

"Collaborate with me today?" she asked Zaiden. "You talk to customers, I restock, we split what Mr. Visver pays us." Zaiden agreed, and they worked the booth in a systematic way: he handed out samples, she refilled the crates, and Mr. Visser paid them each four dollars. Ariana now had fifteen. She wrote the numbers in her own notebook, not shark facts but jar math, and figured the ratio of what she had to what she needed: fifteen out of twenty-two.

The twist came when she went back to the jam booth with her fifteen dollars, planning to ask the vendor to hold the big jar until next Saturday. Aveer was already there, holding the last big jar, digging for coins. Ariana's stomach dropped. Then Aveer turned around and saw her face. "You've been staring at these for a month," Aveer said. "Take it. My mom makes her own jam anyway. I just like the labels."

"But I'm seven dollars short," Ariana said.

"Then owe me," Aveer said, and then hesitated. "Wait. No. My brother owes me money from March and it never ends. Pay me next week, no interest, and we're even." Ariana grinned and set fifteen dollars on the table.

"Sold," said the vendor, sliding the jar into a paper bag.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Emilie was in the game lobby at 7:40, twenty minutes before the clan battle started, when Laurence sent her a screenshot of something strange. It was a photo of the school courtyard, taken that afternoon, and under it someone called DragonVee had written, "Nice spot, Emilie and friends, see you around." Her hands went cold on the keyboard. The courtyard was for clan members only; the courtyard gate had been locked all day; and she had never posted that picture anywhere.

"How did he get a photo of us?" she typed into the lobby chat. Laurence's reply came fast: "I don't know. Elaina says DragonVee knew her street name too."

Emilie thought for a moment. Someone had taken the photo, and someone had found where Elaina lived, but the game chat itself was locked to the clan. She tested her first idea: maybe DragonVee was in the clan under a second name. She scrolled through the member list, comparing join dates and play times, but nothing matched. Then she opened Elaina's profile, and there it was, tiny and gray at the bottom of an old post: a location tag. Elaina had posted from her phone, and the phone had stamped the street name right onto the picture, like a return address nobody noticed. The courtyard photo was stamped too.

"He's not in the clan," Emilie wrote. "He's reading the tags." Then she remembered something she had done on her own phone, fiddling with settings one arid, boring Sunday afternoon: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never. She had set the game to never, months ago, because the constant tracking seemed to hinder the battery. Elaina and Laurence had not.

"Check your game app in location settings," she told them. The battle clock showed eight minutes. Elaina found it first: her game was set to always. She changed it to only while you are using it, and Laurence, checking, found his on always too and switched his to never. Then Elaina deleted the tagged posts, one by one, while the countdown hit its climax and the lobby burst into battle music.

Emilie put on her headset as her character loaded onto the field. DragonVee did not appear in the chat that night, or the next.

"Private lobby tomorrow," Laurence said.

"Private lobby," Emilie agreed, and hit play.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday.
story:
On Friday afternoon, Maelie's mother dropped her at Eleni's house with her overnight bag, because Maelie's parents were driving to the hospital where her grandmother was having surgery on her knee. "They're rebuilding a bit of the cartilage in there," her mother had explained at breakfast, bending her own ear forward to show how bendy that rubbery stuff was. Maelie had nodded, but all day she had carried a tight feeling in her chest, like a stone in a coat pocket.

At Eleni's house the kitchen smelled of chicken and warm bread. Eleni's little brother was setting the table with a blue cloth, and their father was humming. Then, just as the sky outside turned pink and gold, Eleni's mother called out, "Sunset, everyone." Elenie took her mother's phone and slid it into a drawer in the hallway. The tablet went next, and the little brother handed over a handheld game with only a small groan.

"Your phone too," Eleni said to Maelie. "Shabbat starts at sunset on Friday, so screens go away."

Maelie handed it over, then remembered with a jolt that her mother had promised to text after the surgery. She stood in the hallway, listening to her own heartbeat, and tried to perceive the thing Eleni had named, the day of rest, resting all around the house like weather. She could not see it, only its effects: the drawer shut, the humming, the candles Eleni's mother was lighting now.

"How will I know about Grandma?" Maelie whispered.

Eleni thought. "You could call the hospital from their old phone in the den. It's a landline. We're allowed."

Maelie dialed, and a nurse told her the surgery had gone well and her grandmother was already asking for pudding. Maelie walked back to the candles feeling lighter, and ate the best bread of her life.

The next evening, after three stars showed in the darkening sky, Eleni opened the drawer and held out Maelie's phone. "Shabbat ends after nightfall on Saturday," she said. "See? It comes back."

On the screen was a photo of Grandma, awake, waving, influential in her hospital gown like a queen.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Emmett set the plastic container on the lab table and counted the mealworms again. Six larva, each one about two centimeters long, wriggling through a bed of oatmeal. His project compared how fast they grew in a warm tank versus a regular one, because his cousin had told him tropical beetles got huge, and Emmett wanted to know whether heat alone could speed up a larva's growth. Every Monday for five weeks he had measured them with a ruler and written the numbers in his notebook.

"You're going to lose," Kobe said, leaning over the data table. "Graysen built a robot arm."

"A robot arm doesn't answer a question," Emmett said. "Mine does."

The night before the fair, Emmett spread his poster on the kitchen table and tried to articulate what his graph was showing. He had put weeks of growth on the vertical line and the two tanks on the horizontal line, and when he squinted at it, the lines crossed in a way that made it look like the mealworms had shrunk. He read it three times. It said the opposite of what had happened.

He pulled out his notebook and found the page where Ms. Leblanc had written two words beside his question: independent, dependent. The tanks were the thing he had chosen, so that was the independent variable. The growth was what he had measured because of it, the dependent variable. "The independent variable goes on the horizontal x-axis," he said out loud to the kitchen, "and the dependent variable goes on the vertical y-axis." His graph had them swapped. He got a fresh piece of graph paper and started over, plotting weeks along the bottom and average length going up, one careful point at a time.

At the fair, in the science classroom with desks pushed against the walls, Graysen's robot arm stacked three plastic cups and a small crowd clapped. Emmett stood beside his poster and waited. When Ms. Leblanc stopped in front of his graph, she followed the line with one finger, up and to the right.

"So the warm tank," she said.

"Almost twice as fast," Emmett said. "See, the line for the tropical one climbs steeper from week one."

Ms. Leblanc nodded slowly and wrote something on her clipboard. Behind her, Kobe gave Emmett two thumbs up, nearly knocking over the mealworm tank as he did it.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, "Más despacio, por favor" means "More slowly, please," a phrase that helps learners follow a fast answer.
story:
At Khaleesi's kitchen table, Nicolas spread out the wrinkled map of a pretend town Ms. Chan had drawn for their Spanish project. "Okay," Khaleesi said, tapping the paper plaza. "You're a lost tourist. I'm the local. Ask me where the library is."

Nicolas took a breath. "¿Dónde está la biblioteca?"

Khaleesi answered in a rush of Spanish, hands waving left, then right, then somewhere behind her. Nicolas caught the word for street and nothing else. "Whoa, whoa," he said, laughing. "I perceived exactly one direction in all that, and it might have been a sneeze."

From the counter, Khaleesi's older brother snickered. He had been asking invasive questions about the project all afternoon, leaning over their shoulders, and now he offered his opinion: "You should just write everything on your arm before the presentation."

"No, thanks." Nicolas stared at the map. Fast Spanish was the problem, and he needed a real fix, not a cheat. He flipped through the old memoir Khaleesi's grandmother had written, the one they were using for vocabulary because it described her first year in a new country. There, underlined in pencil, was a phrase she had used constantly: Más despacio, por favor. Beside it, in her shaky handwriting: More slowly, please.

"That's it," Nicolas said. He sat up straight and pointed at Khaleesi. "Again. Where's the library? Full speed."

Khaleesi shrugged and let the torrent loose. This time Nicolas raised his hand like a student with an urgent question. "¡Más despacio, por favor!"

The effect was instant. Khaleesi slowed down so much she sounded like a tape player with dying batteries, pointing left at the corner, then right at the blue doors. Nicolas caught every word. fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
The moving truck had obstructed the whole street the day Eleanor left her old house, and she had watched it from the car window until the corner swallowed it. Now it was Tuesday, her third day at her new school, and Ms. Chukwu was assigning seats. Eleanor ended up beside a girl named Lucie, who kept a photo taped inside her pencil case. During silent reading, Eleanor peeked and saw it: a street with symmetrical houses, a mailbox, a dog on a lawn.

" That's my old street," Lucie whispered, and then her eyes went shiny and one tear fell right onto her science worksheet. She wiped it fast, but Eleanor had seen it.

The weird thing came on Thursday. Lucie told a joke about the cafeteria's meatloaf to Angelica, and Angelica laughed so hard she knocked over her milk, and Lucie laughed too, a real laugh with her head tipped back. Eleanor frowned at her desk. How could a person cry over a photo on Tuesday and laugh like that two days later? She opened her notebook and wrote: Lucie moved here last year. Cried then. Laughs now. Why? She had a guess, but guesses needed testing. She decided to test it on herself, and she had a deadline, because Friday was the day Ms. Chukwu collected the pen pal letters for the old school's fourth graders, and Eleanor had promised hers by then.

That night she wrote the letter at the kitchen table.

Dear Angelica and Lucie, she began, then crossed it out and started over. Dear friends from before, she wrote instead. "I keep thinking homesickness works like weather. Everyone says it's the sad feeling you get from being away from home and the people you know, and almost everybody gets it after a move. But here is what I noticed: it doesn't stay. It gets smaller while you're settling in, without asking your permission. Today Lucie laughed at meatloaf. Tomorrow I am going to try laughing at something too, and I will record the result. Scientist's honor, Eleanor."

On Friday morning she handed the letter in early, and Ms. Chukwu read the first lines and smiled at her over the paper. At lunch, Angelica slid a tray next to Eleanor's and pointed at the mystery casserole. "I dare you to try it," Angelica said. Eleanor took one bite, made a face like a startled cat, and both girls cracked up, Lucie leaning over from across the table to see what happened.

Eleanor pulled out her notebook and added a line: Day four, laughed twice. She looked at the photo still peeking from Lucie's pencil case, then at the empty chair beside her where a new friend could sit Monday.

"Homesickness," she said to Angelica, "doesn't stand a chance."
